nameStory: This plant gets its charming name from its fuzzy, hairy leaves that supposedly feel soft like a cat's ear when you run your fingers over them. The scientific name Hypochaeris comes from Greek words meaning "under" and "pig," referring to how pigs were thought to enjoy eating these plants in ancient times.
description: Common Cat's-ear is a low-growing perennial herb that forms flat rosettes of leaves pressed close to the ground, much like its look-alike cousin the dandelion. The whole plant stays quite short, rarely getting taller than 6-8 inches, with bright yellow daisy-like flowers rising above the leaves on slender, mostly leafless stems. Originally from Europe, this hardy little plant has made itself quite at home in New England lawns and grassy areas. Despite being considered a weed in some places, it's actually edible and can add a slightly bitter, chicory-like flavor to salads.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves grow in a flat rosette pattern and are covered with rough, bristly hairs that feel distinctly fuzzy to the touch - this is the key feature that separates it from smooth dandelion leaves. The leaf edges are deeply lobed with rounded teeth.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow composite flowers that look very similar to dandelions, with many thin petals radiating from the center. The flower stems are usually branched (unlike dandelions) and have small scale-like bracts along their length.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading rosettes that hug the ground tightly. The plant rarely grows taller than 8 inches and spreads outward rather than upward, creating circular patches in lawns.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy, white seed heads similar to dandelion puff balls, but often with more feathery, branched bristles that feel softer when blown apart.

habitat: Common Cat's-ear thrives in disturbed soils and is especially fond of lawns, roadsides, fields, and other grassy areas throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both acidic and alkaline conditions, often growing alongside dandelions, plantains, and other common lawn "weeds." You'll find it from sea level up to moderate elevations, particularly in areas that get regular foot traffic or mowing.

seasonality.spring: Fresh leaf rosettes emerge early, and the plant begins its first flush of blooming in late spring. The fuzzy leaves are most tender and noticeable as they contrast with emerging grass.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with bright yellow blooms appearing continuously through the warm months. Seed heads develop and disperse throughout summer, creating new plants nearby.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming into early fall, with seed production slowing down. Leaves remain green and visible, though growth slows as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, the leaf rosettes may persist and stay somewhat green, though they become dormant. In harsh winters, the plant dies back to its root system and re-emerges in spring.

funFact: Despite being called a "false dandelion," Common Cat's-ear is actually more closely related to chicory than to true dandelions, and like chicory, its roots can be roasted and ground as a coffee substitute - early European settlers sometimes used it this way when real coffee was scarce!
confusionNotes: Most people mistake this for a dandelion at first glance, but here's the simple test: run your hand over the leaves. If they feel fuzzy and rough like sandpaper, it's Cat's-ear. If they're smooth and hairless, it's a dandelion. Also, Cat's-ear flower stems usually branch and have small bracts, while dandelion stems are single and smooth.
contextualKnowledge: The name "false dandelion" can be misleading since this plant is actually quite different from true dandelions botanically, even though they look similar. It's also sometimes called "flatweed" because of its ground-hugging growth habit, which helps it survive mowing and foot traffic that would damage taller plants.
compareHints: Common Cat's-ear differs from its relative Smooth Cat's-ear mainly in the hairiness - as the names suggest, Common Cat's-ear has distinctly fuzzy, rough leaves while Smooth Cat's-ear has nearly hairless leaves. Common Cat's-ear is also generally more robust and longer-lived, being a perennial rather than an annual like its smooth cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its much more common relative Common Cat's-ear, Smooth Cat's Ear has completely hairless leaves that feel smooth to the touch rather than fuzzy or rough.
